units.title: Live: storm across the Sound
units.author: soundfm
units.text: 06:10. Good morning. The Met Office's amber wind warning is now in force across the whole of the Marrow Sound and runs until midday tomorrow. Gusts are already passing 45 knots at Carrow Point. Sound Lines has cancelled every sailing this morning. We'll keep this page going all day with roads, power, schools and anything you send us. Please stay in if you can.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 06:55. Schools. Tollinby Primary, Brackwater Primary and the Lisle school are all closed today. The secondary school bus from Gilliver is not running, and the Port Ammet secondary says pupils who can't get in safely should stay at home. Nurseries are making their own decisions; check with yours directly.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 07:40. Roads. A beech is down across the Brackwater ridge road near Holly Lane, and the reservoir road is blocked by fallen trees at the lay-by. The lower Tollinby road is passable with care at Mill Bridge, where branches are down. The Carrow Point road has been shut since last night because of waves.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 08:30. Power. Sound Power Co-op says around 400 properties are off in the Brackwater and Tollinby areas after trees came down on overhead lines. Crews are out but can't work at height in gusts above their safety limit. The co-op asks people not to ring to report a cut that is already listed on its website.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 09:50. The Port Ammet promenade has been closed by the council after waves began throwing shingle onto the footpath. A listener on the harbour sends word that a litter bin has been seen floating upright past the fish quay. We have no further information on the bin.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 11:05. In Weyhaven, tower block lifts across the city have been switched off as a precaution, and the bus operator has suspended routes over the harbour bridge. The city council says its emergency line has taken more than two hundred calls this morning, most about loose roofing and fallen fences.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 12:00. Power update: the co-op now says about 900 properties are without supply, mostly around Brackwater, the ridge road and the east side of Tollinby. Gilliver and Port Ammet are largely unaffected so far. The co-op says some homes may be off overnight.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 13:20. Pictures are coming in. A trampoline from a garden in Tollinby has crossed two fences and landed, perfectly level, on a neighbour's patio. In Lisle, the pier lights are disappearing into spray at every wave. Thank you for sending them, and please take them from indoors.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 14:30. The fire service has helped a driver out of a car stranded in floodwater at the dip in the Tollinby road near the garden centre. He was unhurt and, we're told, was waiting calmly on the roof of the car with a packet of crisps. The road is closed at that point; please use the B-road.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 15:45. The Met Office says its headland station recorded a gust of 59 knots this afternoon and that stronger gusts are likely tonight as the centre of the low passes to the north. Rainfall totals of 40 to 60 mm are possible by tomorrow. Small streams around Brackwater are rising quickly.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 17:20. Gilliver. Waves are overtopping the sea wall on the evening high tide by the lifeboat house, and stones thrown up onto the harbour road have reduced it to one lane. The harbour is closed. The harbourmaster asks people to keep off the front entirely until the tide turns.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 18:40. Power. About 1,200 properties are now off. The co-op says it has restored supply to the pumping station at Brackwater and is working on the Station Road care home in Tollinby next. Brackwater village hall is open with a generator, hot drinks and phone charging until 22:00.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 19:30. The strongest gusts are expected between now and midnight. The Coastguard asks everyone to stay away from sea fronts, slipways and harbour walls, and says there is no reason for anyone to be on the water tonight. Port Ammet General says it has seen a steady stream of minor injuries, mostly from falls.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 20:45. A&E staff are asking people not to go outside after dark to secure loose things. One doctor told us: 'Everything you're trying to save can be replaced. Your wrist takes six weeks.' Several of tonight's patients were hurt holding on to sheds, greenhouses and trampolines.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 21:05. We're closing the live page for tonight; the overnight show will carry updates on air until morning. Tomorrow's ferries: Sound Lines will decide at 06:00. Tomorrow's schools: expect closures again; we'll have the list from 06:30. Keep your phones charged and look in on your neighbours.

units.title: Holm owner issues 'community update' after Courier report
units.author: courier
units.text: Ardent Vale Holdings, the owner of Kittering Holm, has sent what it calls a 'community update' to addresses across the Sound, a day after the Courier reported on the clearance of the island. The message, signed by the company's community team, describes Ardent Vale as committed to 'stewardship' and 'respect' for the Sound.

units.author: courier
units.text: It says that works on the Holm are proceeding 'responsibly and in full accordance with all consents' and repeats that the company has 'no plans to announce at this time'. It does not say what the island will be used for or why the work must be completed in thirty days. Several readers told the Courier they had received the message without having signed up to any mailing list.

units.author: courier
units.text: The Courier has asked Ardent Vale how it obtained residents' email addresses, and has repeated its earlier questions about the future of the Holm. The company had not replied by the time of going to press. Grieve Land Services, which holds the clearance contract, said it had nothing to add to its earlier statement.

units.title: Letters: readers on the Holm
units.author: courier
units.text: From a reader in Gilliver: 'Thank you for yesterday's report. I have looked at the Holm every morning for fifty years and I never thought about who owned it. Now I find I mind very much, and I can't say why, except that it was always there and soon it will be something else. Nobody has asked us what.'

units.author: courier
units.text: From a reader in Tollinby: 'It's their land. They bought it, they got permission, they're paying a local firm to clear it. If they want to grow turnips on it, that's their business. I'd rather the Courier spent its pages on the state of the Tollinby road, which floods every time it rains and which the council does own.'

units.author: courier
units.text: From a reader in Lisle: 'Your article was right about the curing station, and I would add that the women who gutted herring there crossed every morning and came home every night, whatever the weather. Nobody ever stayed out there. I don't know whether that means anything, but it is a fact, and you might print it.'

units.author: courier
units.text: From a retired forester in Port Ammet: 'Thirty days for a whole island is quick, but it isn't mad, with good saws and a crew that knows its business. What would worry me is the weather, the ground and the hours of daylight at this end of the year. I hope whoever is out there is being allowed to stop when the light goes.'

units.title: Tower block residents climb as gales stop city lifts
units.author: weypost
units.text: Thousands of Weyhaven residents faced long climbs today after lifts in the city's tower blocks were switched off as a precaution during the storm. Most high-rise lifts are fitted with wind sensors that halt them when the building's movement in gusts could cause the ropes to swing in the shaft.

units.author: weypost
units.text: Neighbours in several blocks organised themselves to carry water and shopping to older residents on upper floors. In one building a corner shop owner offered torches and candles at cost and a student made repeated trips up fourteen flights with bottled water. 'You find out who your neighbours are on a day like this,' one resident said.

units.author: weypost
units.text: The city council said lifts would be returned to service block by block once gusts eased, which is not expected before tomorrow. It reminded landlords that residents with mobility needs should be contacted directly. Its emergency line remains open through the night.

units.author: weypost
units.text: Elsewhere in the city, the roof of a bus shelter on Quay Road was torn away, and a large section of fencing at the retail park on the ring road blew across a car park. No injuries were reported in either incident. The Quayside night market, cancelled yesterday, will return next week.

units.title: Port at a standstill as cranes stay locked
units.author: weypost
units.text: Weyhaven's container port handled no cargo today for the first time since the last major storm three winters ago. Two ships rode out the gale at anchor in the outer roads, and port staff spent the day checking lashings on stacked containers.

units.author: weypost
units.text: The port's operator said work would resume once gusts had dropped below the cranes' limit for a full hour. Hauliers have been told to expect a backlog, with lorries queuing on the port road for most of tomorrow once the gates reopen.

units.title: Coastal timber haulage halted as storm shuts roads
units.author: tradejournal
units.text: Timber haulage across the coastal north of the region came to a halt today as the storm closed roads and harbours. Hauliers reported trees down on forest roads and log stacks moved by the wind at two depots. One firm said a lorry had been stopped on a ridge road for six hours waiting for a council crew to cut a fallen beech.

units.author: tradejournal
units.text: Island and coastal clearance sites, which depend on boats to move timber and supplies, are expected to lose at least two days. Contractors said the loss of working time could be partly recovered once the weather clears, but that storm-damaged ground and windblown trees would slow felling for some days afterwards.

units.author: tradejournal
units.text: The industry's safety council has repeated its advice that no felling should take place in high winds, whatever the contract deadline. 'Nobody's ever been sued for stopping work in a storm,' its chair said. 'Plenty have been for carrying on.'

units.title: Severe weather: how to make a claim
units.author: lyle_insurance
units.text: Good morning from Lyle Mutual. A severe weather warning is in force in your area. If your vehicle or home is damaged, please make it safe if you can do so without risk, take photographs, and keep receipts for any emergency repairs. Claims can be started online at any time. Peace of mind means knowing we're here when the weather isn't. Small print: excess applies; see your policy schedule.

units.title: Pay statement available: period 2
units.author: grieve_payroll
units.text: Your pay statement for period 2 (contract days 8 to 14) is now available at the site terminal. Contract: Kittering Holm clearance. Day rate per worker: $300. Piece rate: $100 per tree delivered, as recorded on site returns. Reference: GLS-KH-1402. This is an automated message. Please do not reply to this address.

units.title: Outstanding balance at period end (ref GLS-KH-1403)
units.author: grieve_payroll
units.text: Outstanding balance notice. Reference: GLS-KH-1403. Pay period 2 closed with crew wages outstanding on the site account. The balance has been carried into period 3 and reported to Operations. Payments made at the site terminal clear the oldest liabilities first. This mailbox is not monitored.

units.title: Roster change recorded
units.author: grieve_payroll
units.text: Roster change recorded. Reference: GLS-KH-1404. A leaver on the Kittering Holm roster has been included in the period 2 statement. Final pay is calculated to the last recorded day worked. Day-rate liabilities for remaining crew continue at $300 per worker per day. This is an automated message. Please do not reply to this address.

units.title: Press enquiries (please read)
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text:
Hi, the more formal note I promised:
- After yesterday's Courier piece, a reporter may try to contact you or the crew directly.
- Please don't speak to the press, on or off the record, and ask the crew not to either.
- This isn't because there's anything to hide. The client is very hands-off and prefers quiet, and it's simpler if one person speaks for the job.
- If anyone gets in touch, forward it to me and I'll handle it.
Thanks, Ruth

units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi, one addition to this morning. This includes the local forums. Somebody on the Sound Board has already asked who is on the crew, and the admin there removed it, which was decent of him. Please remind the crew not to post about the job anywhere, even to defend it. I know how tempting that is when people are wrong on the internet. Thanks, Ruth

units.title: Storm: today's arrangements
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text:
Hi,
- The supply skipper is watching the Coastguard advice and won't cross while the gale warning stands. Anything on order rolls to his next safe crossing.
- No felling while the warning is in force, and nobody near the shore or under leaning trees. You know this; I'm saying it for the file.
- If comms drop, don't worry about check-ins. I'll assume you're sensibly sheltering.
Thanks, Ruth

units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi, end of day. Head office is fine apart from a flooded car park; the generator came on when the lights went and nobody noticed except the coffee machine. The Met Office says the worst is tonight, with the warning running to midday tomorrow. Just checking where we are on numbers when you have a moment, but honestly, safety first today. Thanks, Ruth

units.title: Fwd: Coastguard advice for island sites
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi, forwarding the Coastguard's note for island and coastal work sites, summarised so you don't have to read four pages: keep everyone above the high-water line tonight and tomorrow morning, because the surge comes on top of spring tides; tie down or bring in anything near the landing; and don't send anyone to check boats or moorings in the dark. Thanks, Ruth

units.title: Period end: wages
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi, the pay period closed today with crew wages still outstanding, so it now shows on the period report that goes to the directors. I'd much rather it didn't. I know the storm hasn't helped and you can't sell timber you can't ship. Even a partial payment at the terminal would let me say it's in hand. Thanks, Ruth

units.title: Re: crew numbers
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi, a follow-up on the crew being short. I asked two agencies this morning whether anyone could go across after the storm. One said no outright. The other asked whether it was 'the Holm job from the paper', and then said they'd ring back, which they haven't. I'll keep at it. In the meantime, please don't stretch the remaining crew to make up the numbers. Thanks, Ruth

units.title: A community update from Ardent Vale
units.author: ardentvale_pr
units.text: Dear friend of the Sound, at Ardent Vale we believe that stewardship begins with listening. We are aware of recent coverage concerning our land at Kittering Holm, and we wish to reassure the communities of the Marrow Sound that our long-term vision is one of respect: for the land, for the water, and for the people who live alongside them.

units.author: ardentvale_pr
units.text: Works on the Holm are proceeding responsibly and in full accordance with all consents. As a patient, responsible owner, we have no plans to announce at this time, and we will share our long-term vision with the community when the moment is right. In the meantime we send our warmest wishes to everyone weathering this week's storm. With regards, The Ardent Vale Community Team

units.title: storm!!
units.author: sam
units.text: hi, the wind took the recycling bin across the whole street and it's sitting in Mrs Abbot's hedge like it lives there now. power flickered twice, Pilot barked at the lights both times like he'd caught them doing something. school's shut so Bea spent all day rehearsing her tree lines at me in the kitchen, in a different accent every time. anyway is it really fine out there? the radio keeps saying 'the islands' in a serious voice. love, S x

units.author: sam
units.text: PS Mum is waiting for the hospital to ring with a date for the hip and says she's 'not fussed', which means she's checked her phone forty times. I'll take her in when it comes, you don't need to do anything except not fall off an island. She asked me to tell you to wear a hat. Consider yourself told. S x

units.author: sam
units.text: can't sleep, the wind is doing the thing with the letterbox. I keep thinking about the bit in the paper where it says nobody has lived out there for a hundred years and then thinking well, somebody does now, and it's you. that's all. that's not a question. go to sleep. S x

units.title: Why did the chainsaw go to therapy?
units.author: hal_brannock
units.text: Chief. It had too many issues to cut through. Road job's off again so I spent the day building a bird table with my nephew. It has a roof, a porch and a lean the boy calls 'character'. If the gale takes it, I'm blaming the council. Hope your lot have something to do indoors that isn't cards with the one bloke who cheats. There's always one. Hal

units.author: hal_brannock
units.text: Also found an old Grieve hi-vis in the shed tonight, from about four contracts ago, with Ruth's laminated site rules card still in the pocket. Rule 7: report all concerns to your supervisor. Rule 8 has been torn off. I don't remember tearing it. Probably used it for a shopping list. Anyway. Bird table's still up. Hal

units.title: heard on the grapevine
units.author: hal_brannock
units.text: Chief, heard on the grapevine one of your lot went home. Happens to the best of us, and it's never about the site lead, whatever they tell you at the time. Long jobs, short days, no pub. Keep the rest fed and keep them together of an evening. Don't take it personal. Hal

units.title: The storm
units.author: ana_reyner
units.text: Hello, sorry. Our block lost its lift this morning and I'm writing on my phone in the kitchen with the radio on, which my mother would say is how all bad decisions get made. I'm fine. Really. Please tell Tomas the balcony door he always worried about has held, and that I've stopped standing next to it. Is he sleeping? Ana

units.title: Is Tomas all right?
units.author: ana_reyner
units.text: I'm sorry to ask this. A woman at work whose cousin knows someone at Grieve said one of the crew had come home from the island. She didn't know who. If it was Tomas he hasn't rung me, and he always rings me, even when he has nothing to say. If it wasn't him, please tell him I'm fine. Either way, I'm sorry to bother you. Ana

units.title: Amber warning in force: wind
units.author: met
units.text: Marrow Sound, 06:00 ST. The amber wind warning is now in force until 12:00 tomorrow. South-westerly severe gale 9, occasionally storm 10 on exposed coasts. Gusts of 55 to 65 knots on headlands, 45 to 50 inland. Danger to life from flying debris and large waves. Avoid coastal paths, sea fronts and harbour walls. Travel only if necessary.

units.title: Forecast: severe gales, heavy rain
units.author: met
units.text: Today: severe gales with heavy rain, persistent at times. Maximum 12 C. Tonight: gales continuing, strongest before midnight as the low centre passes north, veering westerly later. Rain easing to showers. Minimum 8 C. Tomorrow: westerly gale 8, gusting 50 knots on coasts, with squally showers. A brief lull is possible tomorrow evening before further strong winds.

units.author: met
units.text: Warning update, 12:00 ST. Gusts recorded this morning: Carrow Point headland 52 knots, Lisle 49, Port Ammet 44, Brackwater 38. Rainfall 22 mm in six hours at Brackwater. The amber warning remains unchanged. Gusts are expected to increase again this evening, peaking around midnight.

units.title: Coastal flood alert
units.author: met
units.text: Coastal flood alert, Marrow Sound. Spring tides combined with a surge of up to 0.5 m and large waves may cause overtopping of sea defences around the evening high tide (about 18:15 at Gilliver) and tomorrow morning's high tide (about 06:30). Gilliver harbour front, Port Ammet promenade and the Carrow Point road are most at risk. Keep away from sea walls.

units.author: met
units.text: Evening forecast, 18:00 ST. The deepest part of the low is now crossing to the north of the Sound. The strongest gusts, possibly 60 knots or more at Carrow Point, are expected between 21:00 and 01:00. Pressure is expected to bottom out near 971 hPa after midnight. Stay indoors. Winds veer westerly and ease slowly from early morning.

units.title: All sailings cancelled today
units.author: ferry
units.text: Sound Lines, 06:00. All sailings between Port Ammet, Lisle and Gilliver are cancelled today because of severe weather, including tonight's 23:40 and 00:55 night crossings. We will review tomorrow's timetable at 06:00 tomorrow. Tickets for cancelled sailings may be used within seven days or refunded.

units.author: ferry
units.text: Sound Lines, 13:00. Our vessel is safely berthed in the lee at Port Ammet. Crew are on shore standby. Lisle residents with urgent medical appointments in Port Ammet tomorrow should contact the surgery, which is arranging alternatives. We will not be running any service until conditions at the Lisle and Gilliver approaches are safe.

units.author: ferry
units.text: Sound Lines, 19:30. Tomorrow's 07:10 and 09:30 sailings are cancelled. We aim to run a single midday sailing from Port Ammet to Lisle and Gilliver if the morning inspection of the Lisle slip is satisfactory. A decision will be posted by 10:00. Please do not travel to the terminal before then.

units.title: Storm faults: Brackwater and Tollinby
units.author: power
units.text: Sound Power Co-op, 08:00. Trees on overhead lines have cut supply to around 400 properties in the Brackwater area, including the ridge road and the reservoir hamlet, and to parts of east Tollinby. Crews are on site but cannot work at height in gusts above the safety limit. We will update this page every three hours.

units.author: power
units.text: Sound Power Co-op, 13:00. Around 950 properties are now without supply. Priority work: the Brackwater pumping station (restored 12:40) and Station Road, Tollinby, including the care home. Gilliver and Port Ammet supplies are holding. Please report sparking or fallen lines immediately and stay well clear of them.

units.author: power
units.text: Sound Power Co-op, 19:00. About 1,250 properties remain off, mostly on the Brackwater ridge and in east Tollinby, where two poles are down. Some customers will be without power overnight. Brackwater village hall is open with a generator until 22:00. Crews will work through the night wherever gusts allow.

units.title: Roads closed by fallen trees and flooding
units.author: council
units.text: Ammet District Council. Closed: the Brackwater ridge road near Holly Lane (fallen beech), the reservoir road at the lay-by (fallen trees), the Tollinby road at the garden centre dip (flooding), the Carrow Point road (overtopping) and the Port Ammet promenade (shingle). Crews will clear routes when it is safe to use chainsaws.

units.title: Rest centres open
units.author: council
units.text: Ammet District Council. Rest centres are open at Brackwater village hall and Tollinby community hall for anyone without heat or power, with hot drinks, phone charging and blankets. Port Ammet library is open as a warm space until 21:00. If you are worried about a vulnerable neighbour, please call the council's emergency line.

units.title: Storm warning: harbours closed
units.author: coast
units.text: Coastguard, Marrow Sound. Storm warning: south-westerly storm 10 reported at Carrow Point. Gilliver and Lisle harbours are closed to all movements. Port Ammet is closed except to emergency services. Do not attempt to visit, board or adjust vessels on moorings. The public should keep away from slipways, piers and harbour walls.

units.author: coast
units.text: Coastguard, Marrow Sound. Two small vessels have broken from moorings in Gilliver harbour and been recovered. A rowing boat has been reported adrift south of Gilliver and is not being searched for, as it was unoccupied. Mariners should expect floating debris once the storm passes, including fish boxes and timber.

units.author: courier_archivist
units.text: From the front page, 2 February 1953: 'Gale lashes the Sound. Lisle boat stays in. Elms down at Tollinbye.' The Lisle boat did not sail on Saturday or on Sunday. At Tollinbye (sic) eleven elms came down across the Market Road, and the Brackwater road was blocked in three places. At Gilliver the sea came over the harbour wall on both tides. The light at Carrow Point burned throughout, its keepers reporting the worst seas of their service.

units.author: courier_archivist
units.text: The same issue praises two men of the Brackwater estate who cleared the reservoir road 'by lamplight and stubbornness'. A Gilliver correspondent adds that the Holm 'took the full force' and that from the village 'not a light was to be seen upon it, as there has not been these twenty years'. Editor's note: the Holm had been uninhabited since the curing station closed in 1931, so this is less remarkable than it sounds.

units.author: courier_1890s
units.text: A correction. Last week your correspondent repeated a story that the station upon the Holm was once a house of quarantine. We are now informed by Mr Rendle senior, who worked at the curing-house as a lad, that it was never anything but a curing station, and that 'never a sick man went to it, only herring'. We are glad to set the record right, and regret that the gentleman from Port Ammet's grandmother was misinformed.

units.author: courier_archivist
units.text: Editor's note. The correction ran on page 6, a week after the rumour, in noticeably smaller type than the rumour had. It was not repeated. The 'quarantine' story reappeared in a 1958 letter to the editor, in a 1972 holiday leaflet and in a great many places since. As far as I can find, the correction has not been reprinted anywhere between 1911 and today.

units.title: Carrow Point light: log excerpts, winter 1908
units.author: carrow_keeper
units.text: Jan. 12. Middle watch, 00:00 to 04:00. Wind S.W. 8, increasing. Vis. 2 miles in rain. Lamp trimmed 01:00 and 03:00. Clockwork rewound 02:00. Heavy sea on the point. Remarks: assistant reports slates loose on the store roof.

units.author: carrow_keeper
units.text: Jan. 13. Middle watch. Wind S.W. 10, whole gale. Vis. under 1 mile. Lamp trimmed 00:30, 02:30 and 03:45; much spray on the lantern glass. Remarks: two walkers on the shore road below the light at 02:10, going toward Gilliver, no lantern. Hailed from the gallery. Did not answer. Bad night for it.

units.author: carrow_keeper
units.text: Jan. 14. Middle watch. Wind W. 7, moderating. Vis. 5 miles. Lamp correct throughout. Remarks: asked at Gilliver in the forenoon after the walkers. No one out on the road on the 13th by any account, the road being under water at the dip. Entered for the record.

units.title: Gilliver Oral History Project (1976): the window lamp
units.author: oral_history_1970s
units.text: Tape 7, Mrs E. Pascoe. Q: Can you tell us about the lamp in the window? A: Well, everybody did it. You lit it at dusk and you left it till morning. Q: Why? A: For the boats. So they could see the village from the water. [pause] That's what my father said, anyway. Q: And your mother? A: Mother said it was so they'd know the house was awake. I never asked her who 'they' was. You didn't.

units.author: oral_history_1970s
units.text: Tape 7, continued. Q: Did you ever let the lamp go out? A: Once. The winter of the big gale, the oil ran short. [long pause] Father sat up all night in the chair by the window with his coat on. In the morning he bought oil off the Ammet boat at twice the price and never said a word about it. Q: Did anything... A: No. Nothing happened. That's rather the point, isn't it.

units.author: oral_history_1970s
units.text: Tape 8, Mr J. Rendle. Q: Mr Rendle, the same question. The lamp. A: Boats. Nothing else. People make a mystery of it now because they've nothing to do of an evening but watch the television. Q: Your mother kept one? A: Every night. Q: For the boats? A: For my father's boat. And then after he'd gone... [pause] well, she kept it on. Habit. You'd have had to ask her.

units.author: fisher_diary_1930s
units.text: Dec 2. Gale. No boats out. Mended pots in the shed by the lamp all day. Jory came round and sat. Said there was smoke from the old cottage chimney on the Holm, he saw it from the bay yesterday. I said tramps. He said no boat went out. I said then he is mistaken. We had words and he went home without his tea.

units.author: fisher_diary_1930s
units.text: Dec 4. Wind down. Out at six. Lost a fleet of 12 pots on the Holm side, the buoy line cut clean or chafed through, I could not tell which. Two hours looking. New rope 4d a fathom, that is a week gone. Jory would not come. Mother says leave him be, he was always the nervous one.

units.title: Catalogue LBA-0219 (Gilliver, the 1997 gale)
units.author: lowband_archivist
units.text: LBA-0219. Date: winter 1997, during the January gale. Location: Gilliver harbour wall, landward side. Kit: MiniDisc recorder, stereo microphone in a fur windshield. Duration: 48 min. Content: wind roar with frequent overload, halyards, a bell buoy, the wall taking spray. Recordist's note: 'the sea sounds like it's arguing'. Curator's note: heavily overloaded throughout; kept for its historical value and for the bell, which has since been removed.

units.title: Talk: 'no deer on the Holm' (Arnell, 1923)
units.author: hist_wiki_pell
units.text: This claim is poorly sourced. One week's survey late in the season by a single observer is not a census. Red deer swim, and the literature records crossings much longer than nine kilometres. Finding no sign in seven days of mixed weather is what you would expect of a small, wary population. Proposed wording: 'Arnell recorded no deer during a week's survey in 1923.' Not 'the Holm has no deer'.
